projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Louis Leon Ignaszewski was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: (text cut off)--I just need to actually announce a couple of things here. My name is Dave Engen and Caroline, how do you say your last name, Caroline?

sp.speaker: Caroline Meger
sp.p: Meger.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: Meger and Louis, how do I say your last name sir?

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: Ignashefski.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: Okay, we are interviewing Louis Ingnashefski, do I have it?

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: And we are in Easton, Minnesota and it is March the 26th and I think that's everything that I need to announce in that way and just for opening questions, sir, I just wanted to ask um, what branch of the service were you in?

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: CWS.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: CWS, which is,

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: Chemical warfare.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: Okay, okay. And is that a branch of the Army or the Marines?

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: The Army.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: Okay. And that was in World War II,

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: World War II, I was first drafted and left out of Faribault County.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: Really? Well, that was going to be my first question. I think I have everything, don't I Caroline? In terms of,

sp.speaker: Caroline Meger
sp.p: Mm hmm.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: Yeah, so you were drafted then?

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: That's right.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: Could you, and what year were you drafted in?

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: Where were you living at the time? This is Faribault County, right here?

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: Faribault County, we lived out on the farm out here then.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: Okay. So were you pleased to be drafted? Were you,

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: Well, I didn't have any choice.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: You didn't have any choice (laughter).

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: I was the first one that left out of Faribault County.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: Okay. Did you, I'm going to slide this closer to you, that way it will really pick you up nice. Um, were you um, did you know what branch of the service you wanted to go into, or did they just tell you what branch?

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: They just tell you where you are going to go.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: What was it like, I mean, when you, your first days and things in the service, how did that process go?

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: Well, I didn't have any choice. I had to do whatever they told us to do. I was (undecipherable) in Maryland.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: And what kind of things did they tell you to do

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: At the start, we didn't have any choice. We were in chemical warfare service, CWS, and well, we had to do everything that they told us to do. We had our, well, I don't know what you want to call it, our

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: I guess I am not familiar with CWS, what kinds of things did they, were you responsible for? What does that mean, CWS?

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: Chemical Warfare Service.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: I didn't have any idea whether I was going to go or what I was going to do but the first place we went, they sent us to Adrena Arsenal, Maryland.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: And once that you were there, they started to train you in chemical warfare or?

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: Well, more or less.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: Do you remember anything about the training process? About your Boot Camp instructors or anything like that?

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: Not really. I don't remember any of them people anymore.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: Really?

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: That's too long ago.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: (laughter) Yeah. Um, so then you went into World War II, where did you, where did you go? Where did you serve?

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: I went to the first place, we went, we were on maneuvers in New Orleans in Louisiana, we were there for just a couple of weeks. Then we got shipped to Corregidor

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: Okay, and where,

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: in the Philippine Islands.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: Okay. And then from there, is that where you stayed?

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: That's where we stayed. I was in charge of chemicals, of all the chemicals that was used. I guess I knew more about them than anybody else did so that's the job I got.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: So your job was to be in charge of the chemicals that, and what were these chemicals, what were they? What were they used for?

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: Well, they didn't really use any chemicals to start with, that amounted to anything but I was in charge. I had three guys working with me that was under me, I was in charge of them.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: And what kinds of things would you do there? Were you just like,

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: Oh, we was demonstrating chemicals and whatnot, telling what they do. That was before the war started.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: Okay. So, I don't want to ask you anything you are not comfortable talking about, but

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: Oh, I can talk about anything that you want to know.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: (laughter) What were, I guess I'm having trouble figuring out, like what were the chemicals be used against the enemy then?

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: That's right. If, in case there was going to be a war,

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: which they didn't know to begin with, if there was going to be a war or not. Then the Japs, the Japs started war.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: So, this is all before Pearl Harbor that you're in?

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: Oh yeah.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: Okay. Huh. And so then, were the chemicals actually, like what would be an example of a chemical that would be, what would it do? Would it kill people? Would it just stop them? Would it?

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: Well, it was, it would put them to sleep. Really it wasn't anything that would kill anybody, it was like sulfuric acid and

sp.speaker: Caroline Meger
sp.p: Did they end up using that? I mean later on when the war started. Was that used a lot?

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: Oh, I don't know. I didn't get in on any; the war didn't last long enough.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: So, did you um, this seems like kind of a private question but something that we're asking as part of the project, did you see any combat yourself then in World War II?

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: Oh yeah.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: Are you comfortable talking about?

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: It don't make any difference to me.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: Yeah. What combat did you see? Where was it?

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: Well, when they landed on Corregidor, when the Japs landed on Corregidor, I saw that take place there. Most of the chemicals they used there was well, I don't know what you want to call it, it was something that was poisonous and it would put them to sleep.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: And when you say put them to sleep, do you mean put them to sleep permanently or?

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: More or less.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: So, the chemicals would kill the enemy?

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: That's right.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: So was most of your combat dealing with chemicals or did you see combat in a more traditional, you know you think of the war and people shooting at each other and fighting that way.

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: No, I didn't see much of that.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: You didn't see much of that, but you were responsible for coordinating the chemicals that would be used.

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: That's right.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: So do you have a scientific background in things, in this? Was this just something you were good at?

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: Well, I guess I was good at it. That's the reason I got put in there.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: How did they find out that you were good at something like that?

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: I don't know.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: (laughter) Because not many people must have done this kind of job, right?

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: No they didn't.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: How many people do you think did this type of job?

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: Well, there was only four of us that, three guys besides me, and they didn't know, they didn't have no idea of what was taking place at all.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: So, I mean, did you ever then see, like the effects? I mean, you would work with these chemicals, if I am understanding this correctly,

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: and then those chemicals would be used in the war to kill the enemy.

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: That's right.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: And did you ever, were you responsible for administering the chemicals? For making sure that they,

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: Well, we had higher officers that was chemical warfare training and they were the ones that were in charge of, more or less, of what to use them for.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: Okay. So your main job was to prepare them so that they had these chemical weapons to use,

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: That's right.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: when they saw fit.

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: That's right.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: Okay, that makes sense. Yeah. Uh, how often were they used? I mean, was it something that was

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: The war didn't last that long. It only lasted about 3 months.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: The war, okay. You mean World War II, itself or?

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: To start with, yeah.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: To start with. Okay.

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: That's when we got captured then.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: So you got, you were actually a prisoner of war then?

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: Oh yeah.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: Are you comfortable speaking about that?

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: I was a prisoner of war for 3 and a half years.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: Were you really? And who captured you then?

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: The Japs.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: The Japanese. That's a long time, isn't it? To be a prisoner of war?

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: That's right. That's right.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: I mean, if we ask you anything that you are not comfortable talking about but what was that like?

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: Well, we had, we got put in a camp and the same time that we got put into the camp, God, it's so damn long ago already that I forgot most of it.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: Mmm.

sp.speaker: Caroline Meger
sp.p: How were some of the conditions? I mean, were you given, do you remember were you given adequate food? Did they have you working all the time?

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: No, no, no, no, no, no. When the war ended, when we got captured and we got put into prison camp, I got sent to Okinawa. How come I got sent to Okinawa? I don't know. I'll never know what, I don't remember what it was all about.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: Did, so you must have had a lot of friends that you were in there with. I mean, did most people make it out or did a lot of people lose their lives?

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: No, most of them, most of them that I was with would all come back home. We got split up. I was in uh, artillery set up in, let's see, what group was that in? Group 2, I think it was, of the Japs. I got to talking with the Japs and when I got talking with them, they acted just like I should know something. Well, I didn't know. I didn't even know what they were talking about.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: They thought that you should know about the war and what was going on?

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: That's right.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: You were just, you had an important role, but you weren't in on all of the big plans, that's what you're trying to say?

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: No, that's right.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: Were they, I mean, how were they as captors? I mean, you hear, when you read history and things you hear a lot of stories about the Japanese being pretty ruthless at this time to American soldiers.

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: Well yeah, they were but I got along pretty good with them because I got talking so, I got started so I could just, I could understand them and talk to them.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: So were you able to speak some Japanese then?

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: That's right.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: And had you learned Japanese before the war?

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: No, I never did.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: Okay so you just picked up the language?

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: Picked up the language in a hurry.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: So, did you meet people who were your guards, who actually treated you with humanity then?

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: Yeah, we had Big Speedo, what they called, we called him Big Speedo, because he was a bigger man than any of us and he was, he treated us like we were somebody.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: And so you had pretty, I mean, maybe fond memories is a strong word, but he was a human being who was good to you while you were there.

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: He was good to us. There was four of us in the camp that he was in, that he was in charge of. Well, that's about all of these things that I know of.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: Big Speedo, they called him.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: (laughter)

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: What was his proper name? I don't even remember.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Caroline Meger
sp.p: Did you witness, you know, inhumane things happening to other prisoners around you even though you were treated?

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: No, not very much.

sp.speaker: Caroline Meger
sp.p: Not very much.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: Is there anything else that you would like to say about that experience? About being a prisoner of war?

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: Well, there ain't much I can tell you. I don't know. I don't know a hell of a lot about it.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: (laughter) Well, you know a hell of a lot more than we do. (laughter) Did you, what were some of your most, uh, obviously this was one of them but what were some of your most memorable experiences in the war?

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: Well,

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: At any time you want to take a break or anything, we can certainly do that.

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: No, no, no. I don't even remember what we all done.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: (laughter)

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: We had charge of chemical warfare and prison camp life was, well, we was, let's see, what did we do? If you would've asked me this about 5 years ago, I could've told you more.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: Yeah, but this is great though. This is really interesting and it's kind of nice. They'll keep this, keep this stuff around forever, so, Paul Schuster said that you actually drove a jeep for Macarthur, is that true?

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: That's right.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: Could you talk about that? I mean, that's a pretty amazing experience. How did that happen?

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: Well, Macarthur was, he was a major to start with. He wasn't a general.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: He was a major. See there is a magazine laying right down there on the corner, pick it up.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: Should I get it? This one here?

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: Yeah. This just come today, so I ain't,

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: (laughter)

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: Oh here is what they say about Macarthur. He was a, Douglas Macarthur was, he was captured and he was held by the, he was in Clarkfield prison, and he transferred to Honshu Island. He was uh,

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: So he was a prisoner of war in the same place you were?

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: Were you prisoners of war at the same time?

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: Oh sure.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: Oh, really? And this is the Douglas Macarthur that I'm thinking of, right?

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: That's right. That's the only one that I ever knew.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: Yeah. (laughter)

sp.speaker: Caroline Meger
sp.p: Did you ever talk with him when you were in the prison camp?

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: Oh yeah, I talked to him. I talked to him a lot of times.

sp.speaker: Caroline Meger
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: What, I mean, did you know that he was going to become such a significant historical figure?

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: No, no. I didn't know anything about him.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: Did he seem like he would? Did he seem different than the rest of the folks? I mean, not that,

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: Well, I don't think he was any different than anybody else.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: But how come he got picked for general, I don't, well, I can't answer that either.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: Yeah. So how did you end up driving him in a jeep? That was before he became a general?

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: That's right.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: That's an interesting, so did you ever stay in touch with him after, after the war then?

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: Oh yeah. I talked to him, let's see, when was the last time I seen him? We had a reunion. That was a long time after the war was over with.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: Mmm. Did he seem like, kind of a down to earth guy, I mean?

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: Oh yeah. He was okay. There was nothing wrong with him.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: Yeah. That's interesting. Do you have any, we don't need to see them now, but do you have any photographs of you with Macarthur or anything?

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: I don't know if I have them now or not.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: Oh that's okay but that's just an amazing story.

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: I got some, maybe down the basement, I think.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: Yeah. That's amazing. Did you receive any awards or medals or any of those kinds of things?

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: I got all kinds of them.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: (laughter)

sp.speaker: Caroline Meger
sp.p: (laughter)

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: Want to see my uniform?

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Caroline Meger
sp.p: We'll just start at the tape.

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: I'll bring it out.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: Okay. Um, what did you receive a Purple Heart or any of the other awards, what, how did you earn the,

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: The Purple Heart?

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: I got, see I got banged quite a little.

sp.speaker: Caroline Meger
sp.p: Where were you injured?

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: I had all kinds of bruises on me, all over. I had, my hands were, well you can see my hands ain't very good now.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: And so you received the Purple Heart for being,

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: Wounded in the war.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: you get that for being wounded. And what other, do you remember any of the other awards that you received?

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: A Silver Star, outstanding service medal. I got them all in there.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: Purple Heart. Did you ever see a Purple Heart?

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: No, no in fact, when we are done, I would love to see a Purple Heart.

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: Well, it's laying in the box there.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: Okay. And what we want to do to for the tape is you know, since that will be in writing, if there's anything that you want to say about how you earned it or something like that, it can get captured on the,

sp.speaker: Caroline Meger
sp.p: I know you had mentioned you received a Bronze Star, do you know what you received that for?

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: The Bronze Star, I got all kinds of stars,

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: (laughter)

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: All kinds of medals. I knew this fellow here.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: So that's something that you get each month then?

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: Yeah, this is a magazine that comes,

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: Can I look at it for a second?

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: once a month.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: Huh. The Quan, it's called?

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: That's right.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: How did you, unless there is anything else that you want to say about your medals, how did you stay in touch with people here in the states? With your family and friends?

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: I never, they never heard about me from the time I left. When I left to go into the service, they never knew about me until the day I walked in the house when I come home.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: So that must have been just, did they assume that you, that you had been killed?

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: I guess so. All of the neighborhood, the whole neighborhood was surprised to see me when I walked into the house.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: (laughter) I mean, I know this is a long time ago, but do you, so you just, so you just, somehow, you got onto a ship or plane and you came back to Minnesota and you just showed up?

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: That's right.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: (laughter) So how did people react to that? I mean, they must have been thrilled.

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: Well, they were kind of tickled to see me.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: I mean, were your parents alive at that time?

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: My dad was, my mother was dead.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: Did your mother pass while you were in the war?

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: How did he react, do you remember at all? It must have just caught him by,

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: He never got too excited about it.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: (laughter) I think we all have dads like that.

sp.speaker: Caroline Meger
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: Do you remember, but he, do you remember how he met you or did he just say hi, good to see you again? Or,

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: Well, when I come home, the whole neighborhood, all the neighborhood, that was on a Sunday morning when I got home, and all the neighbors were there. All the neighbors from around the area. They was tickled to see me. They didn't know that I was even alive yet.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: So how did they, I mean, did they have a party for you? Did they have a parade?

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: Oh yeah. We had parades.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: For you? Were there other soldiers that came home at the same time or was it just you?

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: No, I was the only one.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: And they had parades for you and everything?

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: Oh yeah.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: How did that feel?

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: Well, just like a, well, I don't know. It was with somebody.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: Mmmm. That's pretty amazing. I can't imagine like, what, do you remember at all, what, I mean, where did you come from? You came from overseas and then did you come into New York or something before,

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: I come from New York and then from New York, no, I didn't come into New York. I come into Seattle, Washington when we landed.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: We come into Seattle, Washington. And there we got on the troop train and we got shipped to Minneapolis.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: What is a troop train exactly? I think I know, but is that just,

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: That's a train with all of the soldiers on it. There was quite a few, I suppose there was a couple hundred of us on there.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: And how were people, I mean, how did they seem to be doing? I mean, they must have been changed men in a lot of ways, or did they seem like young,

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: No, they was okay.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: They were okay. And the parades that they had for you, was that here in Easton?

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: Yeah, more or less.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: Hmm. So, I'm trying to think if there is anything else that we want to ask about the war. Is there anything that we should be asking? (laughter) Is there anything that we are forgetting to ask or anything that you want to say, and again, this is something that will be around for the next couple hundred years.

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: I don't know what I could tell you outside of that it was, when I left, I left and nobody knew where I was going and nobody knew when I come home.

sp.speaker: Caroline Meger
sp.p: Do you remember how you found out that you were going to get to come home? Were you sent a letter or did someone above you tell you that it was time for you to go home?

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: No, we got sent in from, see we got shipped back to Corregidor, and from Corregidor we got on the troop train and then whoever was from Minnesota, we got to come home. I was the only one from Easton. We landed in Minnesota Lake.

sp.speaker: Caroline Meger
sp.p: How was that train ride? I was just curious, you know, the soldiers coming home, was it, was everybody kind of quiet and solemn in their own thoughts?

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: Oh no.

sp.speaker: Caroline Meger
sp.p: Was there a big party on the train?

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: A big party on the train.

sp.speaker: Caroline Meger
sp.p: A big party?

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: (laughter) What year did you return home in?

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: Okay, so the war was over.

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: That's right.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: And where were you when the war ended?

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: I was in, I was in one of the Japanese camps. In one of the Japs camps in uh, oh what do you call that, Nagasaki?

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: So you were in Nagasaki?

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: That's where the bomb was dropped as well.

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: That's right.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: So you were there when the bomb was dropped?

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: That's right.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: What was that like? Did you know that it was? You must have known.

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: We never had any idea what it was until after we found out afterwards.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: So, you know, I've only read about that in the history books, but it was possible to be in that city and not know that the bomb had been dropped?

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: No, that's right. It was dropped on, if they would have hit in the middle of the city, well, I wouldn't be here today but it dropped, they missed it and they got on the outskirts of the town.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: So they were trying to drop it on the middle of the city?

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: That's right.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: So if they had been more accurate, we wouldn't be having this conversation. (END OF TAPE ONE - SIDE ONE) (START OF TAPE ONE - SIDE TWO)

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: (text cut off)--you think that many times that they had an inaccurate uh,

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: Well, we just figured, there was four of us that was together and in Nagasaki and we just were lucky that all four of us, as a matter of fact, two of them live in St. Paul.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: Oh, really?

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: Vernon Fitzpatrick and let's see, what's the, Paul, Paul, Paul Reichert is the other one. The third one, the third one, I don't remember what happened to him. But I got a letter here from, I just got it a couple of days ago, from a fellow in Macon, Georgia that was a buddy of mine.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: Hmm.

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: As a matter of fact, I got the letter here.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: Really?

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: That tells all about it.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: So is that common that people stay in touch after these things?

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: Oh yeah.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: Did you stay in touch with the other three gentlemen or have you stayed in touch over the years with the people that you were with?

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: Well, I haven't been to the Cities very much lately so I suppose. Vernon Fitzpatrick, he's one of them. As a matter of fact, there's a write up in the paper in that magazine there, about him.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: Huh. I'll have to take a look.

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: You can have that magazine if you want it.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: Okay, yeah, I might. Although if it just came, you might want to. I don't want to take your reading away too but hmm, so you were there. I mean, so when you exited, how, how did you, how did they let you out? I mean,

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: The paper is going to fall off,

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: Oh, thank you. How did they let you out?

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: Well, everybody was on their own. When the war was ended, when they dropped that bomb and Japan surrendered, why everybody was on their own then.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: So there was no

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: There wasn't no organization.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: So everybody just left. What about like the guy you talked about, was it Big Speedy or,

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: Big Speedo,

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: Big Speedo.

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: I seen him afterwards. He was an ordinary Jap.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: Hmm. You know, kind of on the lighter side of things, I mean, were there, I mean, I don't know, fun is the wrong word, but how, did you guys have like, I mean, when you guys were in this place for so long, what did, did you have a chance, was it, were there fun moments? Were there entertaining things that you did?

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: Not really.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: Not really. What would you do? How did you spend the day?

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: We spent the day fixing their rifles and whatnot.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: So you had to fix the things that they were using against us,

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: That's right.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: So that must have not been something that you really wanted to do, right?

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: Well, didn't know any better.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: So you really were in, if I'm getting this right, you were in, you started, you went in what year again?

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: What month?

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: In November.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: Okay. So you went in a month before Pearl Harbor,

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: About three months.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: Three months. Okay. And then you were captured about three months after?

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: About three months later.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: And then you were in captivity for the entire war?

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: That's right.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: Okay. Huh. So, what happened and I don't know if there's anything, I mean, this is so interesting. I mean, we really appreciate you sharing your story too, it's going to be really nice to have but I don't know if we have any other questions about the war itself, um,

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: I don't know what I could tell you.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: Yeah. Well, you are telling us a lot but what happened when you got home? You got home and everybody is excited to see you and then where did life go from there?

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: I got home. I was home and then I got send back to Clinton, Iowa. I was in the hospital for three months.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: From?

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: From the war stuff.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Caroline Meger
sp.p: An injury?

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: And what types of injuries, do you remember?

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: Oh, I had all kinds of injuries. I had, I got cut across here, all the way across.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: Do you remember how that happened?

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: Shrapnel.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: Okay. So, yeah we are from MSU and we're doing a Veteran's History Project, just an interview. Unknown voice: You don't have to hurry on my account.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: (laughter) Unknown voice: I will get out of the room.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: (laughter) Is this the gentlemen that takes care of you a bit?

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: That's right. He's my buddy.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: He's your buddy. (laughter)

sp.speaker: Caroline Meger
sp.p: So you said shrapnel cut your chest?

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Caroline Meger
sp.p: Do you have any other?

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: Oh, I got all kinds of marks.

sp.speaker: Caroline Meger
sp.p: Huh.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: Hmmm.

sp.speaker: Caroline Meger
sp.p: It looks like there's something right there.

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: Well, I got a cut there across someplace here.

sp.speaker: Caroline Meger
sp.p: Mm hmm.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: And you said you were in the hospital in Iowa for three months. So they were kind of helping you get on the mend?

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: That's right.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: And then did you come back to Easton after that then?

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: Yeah. I got, about three or four months later, I got discharged.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: And then what did you, I assume that you are retired, right? (laughter) And what did you do?

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: See, I got all kinds of marks on me.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: Oh yeah. Were those just from the fighting itself or just in the camps, people would,

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: No, that was from shrapnel.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: Oh the shrapnel, okay. And so after you were discharged, what did you, and you must have only been, how old were you when you discharged? Do you remember? Early twenties?

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: 46 or 47. 46. 41, 42, 43, 44, 45, 46. I got discharged, I got my discharge papers laying there, on the paper there too, so I can show you that.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: Okay. But you must have been in your early twenties, approximately. When you were discharged?

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: Okay. And what did you do with the rest of your working life and all those kind of things? What kind of job did you do after you got out of the service?

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: I got started at the elevator, the lumberyard had problems getting anybody to work for them, so Harry Heron, he was a lumberman here, he got talking to me and he talked to me and he talked to me,

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: (laughter)

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: so I bought the first truck that the lumberyard had. I done that with just a single axel truck and then pretty soon I had a tandem put on there and then pretty soon I had two semis.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: Wow, so you drove and then you,

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: I drove. I went to Alaska three times.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: No kidding. My father is a retired truck driver, actually.

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: He is?

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: Yep, yep. He drove for Midwest Motor Express up I Minneapolis but uh, yeah. So you became a truck driver, hauling lumber and things,

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: Lumber and freight.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: lumber and freight. Huh, so over the road

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: Over the road. I would be gone sometimes two weeks at a time.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: Okay. And how long did you do that for?

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: Oh, a long time.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: A long time.

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: I done that for a long time. Twenty years.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: Okay. And did you do any working after you stopped driving truck?

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: No, I wasn't able to. I wasn't able to because I had a knee put in. I had three hips put in. That's how come I'm walking around with this here.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: (laughter) Yeah, that will

sp.speaker: Caroline Meger
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: You had talked some about some of the reunions and things and um, did you and do you still go? And did you used to go to the reunions? Could you tell us a little about it?

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: I used to go to them but not anymore. I haven't been to one in the last three or four years.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: Okay. What were they like?

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: Well, everybody was tickled to talk to you, to talk to everybody. They was, they talked about everybody and wanted to know everybody's history.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: What do you do? What are you doing? What do you do nowadays?

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: Where would they be? Would they be in different places?

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: Oh yeah. One in Minneapolis and Clinton, Iowa, Fort Dodge, Iowa, that's where some of the guys were from.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: So that's one.

sp.speaker: Caroline Meger
sp.p: How often were your reunions? Were they like a yearly thing or every couple of years or it just depended on who got it together?

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: It depends on if anybody had enough ambition enough to start one up.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: (laughter)

sp.speaker: Caroline Meger
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: What kind of things would people do? Would you just meet at, would it be a formal event or would you meet at a bar or?

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: Oh we met most of the time, in the hotels.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: We stayed in the Nicollet Hotel in Minneapolis.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: Oh, really?

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: And God, I don't remember all of the places.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: Sure. Sure. But they were pretty important things, I would assume.

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: That's right.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: Wanting to go back and see everybody.

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: Everybody was tickled to see each other.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: There would be maybe 40 or 50 there.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: And did these end up being some of your best friends in life?

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: That's right.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: From the war, yeah. Well, I don't know. I think that might be everything unless there's something that we didn't cover that you would like to include. You have, I mean, obviously it's a fascinating story and we really appreciate you sharing it.

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: No, I don't know what else I could tell you.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: You could ask me about five years ago, I could've told you a lot more.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: Yeah, that would've been great but this was really great too. So, it really was. And how old are you sir, if you don't mind me asking.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: 87. Well I think what I'll do is, is turn off the tape now and if you were willing, I would love to see the Purple Heart and take a couple of pictures.

sp.speaker: Louis Leon Ignaszewski
sp.p: Oh sure.

sp.speaker: David Engen
sp.p: And we'll let you get on with your day.(END OF TAPE ONE - SIDE TWO)
